conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim that giving children more vaccines causes more autism is not supported by the evidence and that peer-reviewed evidence weighs against an increased autism risk. Thus, it rejects the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that giving children more vaccines causes more autism is not supported by the evidence in the provided results.

The most directly relevant study measured *cumulative vaccine antigen exposure*—the antibody-stimulating proteins and polysaccharides received from birth through 23 months, using immunization registries and medical records. It found no increased risk of autism, including autistic disorder or autism with regression, with greater exposure. This addresses the “too many, too soon” mechanism more directly than simply counting appointments or injections.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/

A 2014 evidence-based meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies likewise concluded vaccines were not associated with autism. The supplied results describe its evidence base as five cohort studies totaling more than 1.2 million children and five case-control studies involving more than 9,000 children.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/

For MMR—often central to this allegation—a large Danish nationwide cohort study found no association between MMR vaccination and autism. The search results also state that epidemiologic studies found no increased risk even among children with an older sibling with autism, a group at higher baseline familial risk.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30831578/  
https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/94462

Some provided results assert correlations between rising autism diagnoses and vaccine doses or report vaccinated-versus-unvaccinated comparisons. Those claims do not, from the supplied descriptions, establish causation or show adequate control for differences in healthcare use, diagnosis, family characteristics, and other confounders. Population trends alone are especially weak evidence for an individual causal effect.

Overall, the better-described peer-reviewed cohort, case-control, and meta-analytic evidence weighs against an autism risk increase from greater childhood vaccine exposure.
